walkthroughs.body_html:
Introduction to Economics — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Introduction to Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Introduction to Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a factor of production?
options: Land
Labour
Money
Enterprise
The price of bread
The whole economy
A single firm's profits
A consumer's choices

mcqs.q: What is the difference between revenue and profit?
options: Revenue is total income from sales (price x quantity); profit is what remains after deducting costs from revenue.
Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.
Revenue and profit mean the same thing.
The invisible hand refers to government regulating the economy secretly.

mcqs.q: What did Adam Smith mean by the 'invisible hand'?
options: That individuals pursuing their own self-interest in competitive markets can unintentionally produce socially beneficial outcomes through the price mechanism.
Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
Adam Smith believed all selfish behaviour always benefits society.
The invisible hand refers to government regulating the economy secretly.

mcqs.q: How does raising interest rates reduce inflation?
options: Higher interest rates directly force shops to lower their prices.
Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reducing consumption and investment — lowering aggregate demand and slowing price rises.
Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.
